description: We’re building an educational space game where children explore real astronauts’ missions through interactive comics, animations, and challenges. We’re looking for developers, designers, illustrators, animators, writers, and space researchers. Join us!
summary:
We developed AstroKid, a playable 3D educational game where young learners take on expeditions on the Moon and Mars. Players check equipment, drive rovers, use scientific instruments, collect samples and data, and decide which objectives to pursue. The Apollo 12–inspired expedition draws on NASA mission records and measured lunar terrain. Two fictional expeditions give learners a chance to apply similar skills in new situations.

AstroKid addresses the challenge by giving learners a way to use space science to make decisions and see their consequences. A mission can spark a question about how an instrument works or why an astronaut collects a sample. Learners can follow those questions at their own pace, building confidence and connecting what they experience in the game with the work of real space exploration.
details:
AstroKid is a playable 3D educational game where young learners take on expeditions on the Moon and Mars. Players choose a mission, check their equipment, operate rovers and instruments, collect samples or science data, and decide which objectives to pursue. Optional tasks ask them to weigh additional science work against the resources they need to return safely. Afterward, a debrief records what they accomplished so they can reflect on their choices.

The game links space science to decisions learners can make and see play out. In the Apollo 12–inspired expedition, NASA mission records guide the tasks, and lunar elevation data from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera shapes the terrain. SELENE and ARES use fictional scenarios to let learners apply similar ideas to new problems. Combining measured terrain, historical work, and fictional problem-solving gives learners several ways to engage with space science.

We built the game in Unreal Engine 5 using C++ and Blueprints for game logic, and UMG and Slate for the interface. We adapted 3D assets and used procedural posing for astronaut interactions. The playable version runs offline on Windows PCs. AI tools assisted with development, asset preparation, and documentation.

We considered scientific accuracy, how much information a first-time player can handle, and how to give learners room to make their own decisions. We simplified procedures, kept objectives and feedback clear, and identified which elements come from NASA sources and which were created for the game. We want young learners to feel comfortable trying things, asking questions, and deciding what they want to explore next.
